papers.title: Plann3r: Predicting Planning Costs Grounded in 3D
papers.matched_title: Plann3r: Predicting Planning Costs Grounded in 3D
papers.abstract: Planning paths or trajectories for robot navigation requires understanding scene geometry and traversability. Classic approaches relied on accurate 3D maps to define occupancy based planning costs. Learning based alternatives predict planning costs either in terms of distance to goal or temporal distance between images. However, the former overfits to scene layout and the latter lacks geometric understanding. Moreover, most of these methods estimate \textit{image-level} scalar costs, which are not sufficiently informative to effectively guide the robot. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Plann3r} as a 3D grounded method to predict \textit{pixel-level} planning costs in terms of geodesic distances for any given set of images with an arbitrary subgoal pixel. We integrate Plann3r within a navigation pipeline, dubbed \textbf{VGGT-Nav}, in two unique ways: the offline mapping cum global planning phase iteratively uses Plann3r to generate subgoals and reference image global costmaps; and in the execution phase Plann3r performs simultaneous localization and local planning to generate planning costmaps to directly condition a learnt control policy. We show that the proposed Plann3r and VGGT-Nav largely outperform baselines respectively on the planning and navigation tasks on existing benchmark dataset. We further show real world demonstrations that highlight sim-to-real deployment. We will make the code publicly available: \url{https://plann3r.github.io/} (anonymized).

papers.title: Scaled Preference Conditioning for Terrain Costmap Generation
papers.matched_title: Scaled Preference Conditioning for Terrain Costmap Generation
papers.abstract: Successful autonomous robot navigation in off-road domains requires the ability to generate high-quality terrain costmaps that are able to both generalize well over a wide variety of terrains and rapidly adapt relative costs at test time to meet mission-specific needs. Existing approaches for costmap generation allow for either rapid test-time adaptation of relative costs (e.g., semantic segmentation methods) or generalization to new terrain types (e.g., representation learning methods), but not both. In this work, we present \textit{scaled preference conditioned all-terrain costmap generation} (\textsc{spacer}), a novel approach for generating terrain costmaps that leverages synthetic data during training in order to generalize well to new terrains, and allows for rapid test-time adaptation of relative costs by conditioning on a user-specified \textit{scaled preference context}. Using large-scale aerial maps, we show that \textsc{spacer} achieves the lowest \textit{regret} across varied preferences in five of seven environments for global path planning and generates costmaps from the RELLIS dataset with up to 13\% lower mean absolute error when compared to the ground-truth costmap than the next best methods.

papers.title: From Imitation to Alignment: Human-Preference Flow Policies for Long-Horizon Sidewalk Navigation
papers.matched_title: From Imitation to Alignment: Human-Preference Flow Policies for Long-Horizon Sidewalk Navigation
papers.abstract: Autonomous long-horizon sidewalk navigation is essential for micro-mobility applications such as robotic food delivery and assistive electronic wheelchairs. Unlike autonomous driving on the road, long-horizon sidewalk navigation requires precise maneuvering through unpredictable sidewalk terrains and pedestrians, with a lightweight perception stack as minimal as a single monocular RGB camera. While imitation learning (IL) from demonstrations offers a practical solution, the resulting autopilot policy often suffers from compounding errors, a lack of social compliance on sidewalks, and deficiencies in counterfactual reasoning to handle complex situations. To address these challenges, we introduce FlowPilot, a mapless navigation policy that achieves robust and efficient long-horizon navigation performance using only a monocular RGB camera. We first propose to use anchored flow matching as an action representation for policy pre-training on large-scale robot fleet data and to capture the diverse, complex, multimodal distribution of sidewalk navigation behaviors. To bridge the gap between imitation and alignment, we further design a human-in-the-loop preference learning scheme to tune the policy on a small amount of human intervention data. It strengthens the model's counterfactual reasoning and social compliance on sidewalks. We evaluate FlowPilot through extensive simulation and real-world experiments in diverse sidewalk environments. FlowPilot achieves 42% success rate and 66% route completion in simulation, while FlowPilot-HP further improves real-world robustness and social compliance, reducing IR by 40.0% and NIR by 52.1% relative to the base model. Code and model will be made available.

papers.title: TopoUrbanBench: Group-Structural Compliance Evaluation for Urban Robot Navigation
papers.matched_title: TopoUrbanBench: Group-Structural Compliance Evaluation for Urban Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: Evaluation practice in social robot navigation rests largely on geometric metrics that treat pedestrians as independent obstacles, assuming social compliance is well-approximated by spatial separation from individuals. As robot navigation transitions to complex urban scenarios, the limits of this assumption become apparent: many pedestrians move within social formations rather than as independent individuals, so a trajectory that keeps safe distance from every individual may still bisect a queue or cut through a gathering's interactional core. To make this gap measurable, we present TopoUrbanBench, an evaluation framework for urban robot navigation. First, we define social structure as an intention-driven graph at generation time and measure trajectory intersection with this graph through three group-structural compliance metrics, one per archetype. Second, built on CARLA, we procedurally generate pedestrian formations anchored to urban semantic features under three archetypes---stationary gatherings, goal-anchored queues, and frame-mobile cohesive walking groups. Third, we apply this framework to evaluate vision foundation models and online RL agents, diagnosing where geometric proficiency and structural compliance diverge. Evaluations on a real-world social navigation dataset highlight the persistent challenges of group-structural compliance, exposing the limitations of current models in physical environments. The full generation pipeline is released to enable extension beyond our predefined scenarios.
keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning

papers.title: GRACE: Group-Aware Socially Compliant Visual Navigation in Human Environments
papers.matched_title: GRACE: Group-Aware Socially Compliant Visual Navigation in Human Environments
papers.abstract: Visual navigation has made substantial progress in learning goal-reaching policies from egocentric observations. Most existing approaches primarily focus on geometric traversability, however, they do not explicitly account for the social constraints induced by human-populated environments where collision-free space can still be socially occupied, such as the space between walking partners or within conversational formations. To address this, we present GRACE, a group-aware framework for socially compliant visual navigation. The key insight of GRACE is to explicitly model social relations and group interaction spaces, allowing the robot to avoid paths that are physically feasible but socially undesirable. Specifically, our social perception module builds a visual pedestrian--robot graph from RGB observations and uses soft F-formation targets to supervise group-aware attention. This social representation guides a visual trajectory generator, which we further finetune using group-relative reward-weighted flow matching to preserve personal and group spaces. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 demonstrate that GRACE significantly reduces group-space intrusions and collision events compared with representative baselines, while maintaining competitive navigation efficiency.

papers.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
papers.matched_title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes.

papers.title: Schrödinger's Navigator: Imagining an Ensemble of Futures for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
papers.matched_title: Schrödinger's Navigator: Imagining an Ensemble of Futures for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) requires robots to find target objects in unseen environments without task-specific fine-tuning or pre-built maps, a key capability for general-purpose service robots. Yet methods that perform well in simulation often degrade in cluttered real-world scenes with severe occlusion and latent hazards, where large unseen regions make single-scene inference brittle and unsafe. We propose \textbf{Schrödinger's Navigator}, a belief-aware framework that reasons at inference time over multiple \emph{trajectory-conditioned imagined 3D futures}. Given candidate paths, a trajectory-conditioned 3D world model predicts hypothetical observations and maintains a superposition of plausible scene realizations rather than committing to one map. An adaptive occluder-aware sampler directs imagination to uncertainty-critical regions, while a \emph{Future-Aware Value Map} (FAVM) aggregates imagined futures for robust, proactive action selection. Experiments in simulation and on a physical Go2 quadruped show that Schrödinger's Navigator outperforms strong ZSON baselines, improving hidden-target discovery and risk-aware waypoint selection in occlusion-heavy navigation scenarios. These results highlight imagined 3D futures as a scalable and generalizable strategy for zero-shot navigation in uncertain real-world environments.

papers.title: Task-Aware Environment Augmentation for Reliable Navigation via Shielded Conditional Diffusion
papers.matched_title: Task-Aware Environment Augmentation for Reliable Navigation via Shielded Conditional Diffusion
papers.abstract: Reliable trajectory planning under partial observability depends not only on computing a feasible geometric path, but also on whether the robot receives informative observations while executing that trajectory. Existing approaches usually keep the environment fixed and adapt the robot through belief-space planning, active localization, or added sensing, often incurring costly uncertainty propagation and brittle behavior in observation-poor regions. We flip this perspective and address the largely open problem of \emph{task-aware environment augmentation}: given a mapped environment, a planned task trajectory, and a small budget of visual fiducial markers, where should the environment be augmented so that the planned trajectory can be executed reliably under uncertainty? Our key observation is that useful marker layouts are defined by the localization support they provide along the task trajectory: a small number of well-timed observations can be sufficient to prevent uncertainty from accumulating in regions where state-estimation error would otherwise compromise control. Building on this observation, we present SCoDA, $\textbf{S}$hielded $\textbf{Co}$nditional $\textbf{D}$iffusion for Environment $\textbf{A}$ugmentation. SCoDA learns a conditional distribution over high-performing fiducial layouts from data, using the environment, planned trajectory, disturbance context, and desired execution profile as conditioning. Its shielded sampler reasons over where along the planned execution pose corrections should occur, and steers this distribution toward task-relevant, finite-budget augmentations. Across simulated benchmarks and hardware deployments, we show that SCoDA improves trajectory execution reliability and completion time over strong baselines.

papers.title: MessyNav: Zero-Shot Navigation via Manipulation in Messy Environments
papers.matched_title: MessyNav: Zero-Shot Navigation via Manipulation in Messy Environments
papers.abstract: Real-world environments are messy. Paths are often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring interactive navigation (the ability to alter the environment to clear a path) rather than standard navigation alone. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scenario instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to push, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Deployed on a mobile manipulator across multiple real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav achieves substantially higher success rates than existing baselines without any task-specific training.

papers.title: NavVerse: Benchmarking Indoor-to-Outdoor Embodied Navigation in Continuous Robot Simulation
papers.matched_title: NavVerse: Benchmarking Indoor-to-Outdoor Embodied Navigation in Continuous Robot Simulation
papers.abstract: Robots deployed in delivery, campus, and emergency-response settings often need to navigate from buildings to streets within a single continuous episode. Existing benchmarks usually evaluate indoor and outdoor navigation separately, and many abstract away robot execution, leaving exit finding, boundary traversal, adaptation, and kinodynamic failures underexplored. We introduce Navverse, a physics-enabled benchmark for indoor-to-outdoor embodied navigation. Navverse contains 100 indoor scenes, 50 urban outdoor scenes, and 50 indoor-to-outdoor scenes, and supports Object Navigation, Vision-and-Language Navigation, and Place Navigation tasks, where agents search for semantic points of interest such as restaurants or banks. Agents are evaluated through executable robot interfaces using task-success, path-efficiency, and safety metrics. Zero-shot experiments with RL, VLA, and modular baselines show that current agents remain far from solving cross-context navigation: end-to-end VLAs obtain the highest zero-shot success, while modular method provides the strongest safety profile. PlaceNav further reveals a clear drop from outdoor to indoor-to-outdoor scenes, indicating that adaptation remains major bottlenecks.

papers.title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
papers.matched_title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
papers.abstract: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: early-stage fire localization and invisible gas-leak localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy substantially outperforms diverse baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: PathPainter: Transferring the Generalization Ability of Image Generation Models to Embodied Navigation
papers.matched_title: PathPainter: Transferring the Generalization Ability of Image Generation Models to Embodied Navigation
papers.abstract: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) images have been widely demonstrated to provide valuable prior information for navigation. Given the global information provided by such views, two key challenges remain: how to fully exploit this information and how to reliably use it during execution. In this paper, we propose a navigation system that uses BEV images as global priors and is designed for ground and near-ground robotic platforms. The system employs an image generation model to interpret human intent from natural language, identify the target destination, and generate traversability masks. During execution, we introduce cross-view localization to align the robot's odometry with the BEV map and mitigate long-term drift in conventional odometry. We conduct extensive benchmark experiments to evaluate the proposed method and further validate it on both quadruped robot and UAV platforms. Using only a conventional local motion planner, the robot successfully completes a 285-meter outdoor long-range navigation task. This work demonstrates how the world-understanding capabilities of foundation models can be transferred to embodied navigation, enabling robots to benefit from the strong generalization ability of existing image generation models.

papers.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.matched_title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework. We open-source our code for benchmarking.

papers.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.matched_title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. This open-ended interface, however, exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious driver may issue dangerous ones by design. We first construct a suite of benchmarks that evaluate VLA models along three axes: (i) safe navigation following, (ii) navigation-scene conflict awareness, and (iii) robustness to adversarial instructions, revealing that existing policies are deficient on both safe following and conflict awareness. Guided by these observations, we propose SafeDriveVLA, which decouples conflict reasoning from action generation through an interpretable conflict prediction before the action generation, together with navigation-conditioned world model dreaming that exposes whether the instructed maneuver is feasible before the policy commits. SafeDriveVLA reaches state-of-the-art 83.64 DS and 59.82% SR on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 48.7%, and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 66 to 45 compared to prior state-of-the-art.

papers.title: PIGEON: VLM-Driven Object Navigation via Points of Interest Selection
papers.matched_title: PIGEON: VLM-Driven Object Navigation via Points of Interest Selection
papers.abstract: Object navigation in unseen indoor environments requires agents to perform semantic search under partial observability. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide strong semantic-spatial priors for this task, but how to interface them with robot navigation remains challenging: dense VLM inference is expensive, while abstracting environments into symbolic memories often separates high-level reasoning from the raw visual evidence that supports it. We propose we propose PIGEON (Point of Interest Guided Exploration for Object Navigation), a VLM-driven framework that formulates object navigation as raw-observation-grounded sparse decision problem. PIGEON introduces Points of Interest (PoIs) as sparse visual decision units that couple geometrically executable waypoints with raw egocentric observations. Rather than using VLMs as dense controllers or restricting them to frontier ranking, PIGEON enables VLMs to select among task-critical PoIs, including exploration frontiers, suspected target objects, traversable stairs, and floor-level summaries, while low-level planners execute continuous motion between them. This PoI interface further makes high-level navigation decisions verifiable, allowing us to develop an RLVR pipeline that improves local VLMs without manual Chain-of-Thought annotations. Extensive experiments on Habitat ObjectNav benchmarks show that PIGEON achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, scales consistently with foundation model capacity, and transfers to Active Embodied Question Answering with only prompt modifications. Real-world deployments on physical robots further demonstrate its robustness and efficiency.

papers.title: IntentNav: Learning Spatial-Visual Object Navigation from Human Demonstrations
papers.matched_title: IntentNav: Learning Spatial-Visual Object Navigation from Human Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Object navigation requires a robot to search for an unobserved target in an unknown environment by deciding where to explore next under partial observability. Effective search resembles human-like exploration: selectively probing visually promising frontiers while relying on spatial memory to avoid redundant revisits. We propose IntentNav, a spatial-visual imitation framework that learns human-like ObjectNav policies from human demonstrations. To infer high-level search intent from low-level human actions, we introduce Frontier-based Human-Intent Labeling, which looks ahead in human demonstrations and labels the frontier that best explains the demonstrator's future search direction. We construct a spatial-visual candidate space, where BEV memory tracks explored regions, unexplored frontiers, and trajectory history, while egocentric visual memory provides semantic cues for each candidate. A VLM policy is trained to select among these grounded candidates, using Intent-Aligned Objective to encourage consistent and human-like exploration. IntentNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MP3D, HM3D-v1 and HM3D-v2 ObjectNav benchmarks. The proposed candidate-level navigation interface transfers zero-shot to wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid robots without further VLM fine-tuning. \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/w/IntentNav/}{Project page}.

papers.title: One-Step World Models for Multi-Modal Goal Navigation
papers.matched_title: One-Step World Models for Multi-Modal Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: World-model-based planning is a promising direction for robot navigation because it enables explicit prediction of future observations under candidate actions. However, existing navigation world models typically rely on multi-step diffusion and autoregressive frame generation, which substantially increases model-side latency and complicates closed-loop deployment. In this work, we present a lightweight one-step world model for navigation built on a 3D U-Net with efficient spatial-temporal attention. The model predicts all future frames non-autoregressively in a single pass, while pretraining and random trajectory sampling improve performance in limited-data settings. We integrate this world model into a unified planning framework that supports image-goal, language-goal, and point-goal navigation through modality-specific scoring functions and anchor-based trajectory initialization. Extensive closed-loop experiments in both simulation and real-world environments show that the proposed approach improves generation efficiency and achieves strong navigation performance against state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Training Generalist Navigation Policies via Action Self-Distillation
papers.matched_title: Training Generalist Navigation Policies via Action Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by 30% in indoor settings, 30% on multi-stage tasks, and achieves 95% success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.

papers.title: Teaching Robots Like Dogs: Learning Navigation in Cluttered Scenes from Luring, Gesture, and Speech
papers.matched_title: Teaching Robots Like Dogs: Learning Navigation in Cluttered Scenes from Luring, Gesture, and Speech
papers.abstract: We propose LURE, a framework that lets users teach a quadruped robot new navigation skills in cluttered scenes by physically luring it with a teaching rod, so that the robot then responds to high-level gesture and verbal commands. Achieving this raises two challenges. First, physical teaching is data-burdensome, and social cues vary substantially across users. Therefore, the system should be able to quickly adapt to each new user. Second, the choice of social-cue modality is critical, as verbal commands specify the action while gestures specify the spatial target, where neither alone is sufficient in our setting. LURE addresses both challenges by combining data augmentation via scene reconstruction and multimodal conditioning. For the data burden, we reconstruct each recorded interaction scene in simulation and learn to recover from deliberately injected perturbations, expanding a few minutes of physical interaction into a larger training distribution. For the modality challenge, we condition the policy on both gesture and verbal cues, and show that the two complement each other, jointly outperforming either modality used alone. Overall, LURE achieves a 97.15% success rate in reconstructed-simulation evaluations of six navigation scenarios in cluttered scenes, using less than one hour of real-world demonstrations. We further show that LURE adapts to a novel user from under five minutes of additional real-world interaction, raising sim-evaluated success by 22.23% on average. We additionally deploy LURE on real hardware for a multi-obstacle course combining training scenes unseen together during training.
keywords: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction

papers.title: CostNav: A Navigation Benchmark for Real-World Economic-Cost Evaluation of Physical AI Agents
papers.matched_title: CostNav: A Navigation Benchmark for Real-World Economic-Cost Evaluation of Physical AI Agents
papers.abstract: Current navigation benchmarks focus on task success but do not capture the economic constraints essential for commercializing autonomous delivery systems. We introduce CostNav, an Economic Navigation Benchmark that evaluates physical AI agents on a cost-revenue and break-even analysis, pairing Isaac Sim's collision and cargo dynamics with industry-standard data such as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings and Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) injury reports. To our knowledge, CostNav is the first physics-grounded economic benchmark to use regulatory and financial data to quantify the gap between navigation metrics and commercial deployment, revealing that high task-success rates alone do not ensure economic viability. Evaluating seven baselines (two rule-based and five imitation-learning methods), we find no method economically viable: all yield negative contribution margins. CANVAS, using only an RGB camera and GPS, attains the highest task success and the least-negative margin among methods with non-zero Service-Level Agreement (SLA) compliance (-\$28.40/run), outperforming LiDAR-equipped Nav2 w/ GPS (-\$37.34/run). A sim-trained policy evaluated on a real delivery robot yields SLA compliance close to its simulation result, indicating that policy performance in CostNav's simulation transfers to real-world deployment. We challenge the community to achieve economic viability on CostNav, which scores methods by cost-revenue outcomes.

papers.title: One Agent to Guide Them All: Empowering MLLMs for Vision-and-Language Navigation via Explicit World Representation
papers.matched_title: One Agent to Guide Them All: Empowering MLLMs for Vision-and-Language Navigation via Explicit World Representation
papers.abstract: A navigable agent must understand both high-level semantic instructions and precise spatial structure. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), with their strong generalization, are a promising foundation for such agents. We propose a decoupled design that separates low-level spatial state estimation from high-level semantic planning. Unlike prior methods that rely on predefined, oversimplified textual maps, we introduce an explicit metric world representation that maintains rich and consistent information, allowing the MLLM to query and reason over it for decision-making. We further introduce counterfactual reasoning to elicit the MLLM's capacity, while the world representation ensures the physical validity of the produced actions. We conduct comprehensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments. Our method establishes a new zero-shot state-of-the-art, achieving 48.8% Success Rate (SR) on R2R-CE and 46.2% on RxR-CE. To validate the versatility of our representation, we further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer across diverse embodiments, confirming that the decoupled framework deploys robustly on real robots.

papers.title: CoSMO: Conformal Semantic Mapping for Open-World Safe Robot Navigation
papers.matched_title: CoSMO: Conformal Semantic Mapping for Open-World Safe Robot Navigation
papers.abstract:
Safe autonomous navigation requires not only geometric obstacle avoidance but also semantic awareness. Different object categories demand different safety clearances, and the set of relevant categories may expand as the robot explores novel environments.  
Vision-language models (VLMs) offer rich semantic representations for building maps of unknown scenes, yet their confidence scores are poorly calibrated, making raw predictions unreliable for safety-critical planning. Conformal prediction (CP) can provide coverage guarantees, but existing methods assume a fixed label set and stationary data, limiting their use in open-world settings. We propose Conformal Semantic Mapping for Open-World Safe Robot Navigation (CoSMO), a semantic safety mapping framework that transforms VLM embeddings into calibrated coverage sets and safety-aware obstacle dilations over a dynamically expanding hazard vocabulary, even under distribution shift. Experiments on the Matterport3D (MP3D) dataset show that CoSMO reduces semantic collisions by 61.6% relative to a geometry-only baseline, while maintaining formal coverage guarantees even under delayed expert feedback. Code will be released upon publication.

papers.title: CoGeL: Constraint-to-Geometry Learning from Demonstrations and Failures for Safe Long-Horizon Robot Navigation
papers.matched_title: CoGeL: Constraint-to-Geometry Learning from Demonstrations and Failures for Safe Long-Horizon Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: Robots are often deployed in environments where safety must be learned from experience rather than specified in advance. Demonstrations, operator interventions, near misses, and failed rollouts can reveal which behaviors are risky, but they provide only local evidence. The key challenge is not only to identify risky behavior, but to make that knowledge shape the distance a robot uses for long-horizon planning. Existing goal-conditioned methods can compose short behaviors into longer plans, but they usually assume the safety-relevant cost is already known. We introduce CoGeL, a constraint-to-geometry learning method that learns a soft safety signal from robot data and incorporates it directly into the goal-reaching distance used for planning. This makes the learned distance safety-aware, instead of treating safety as a separate classifier, hard mask, or post-hoc filter. We show that errors in the learned safety signal lead to controlled changes in the navigation geometry, that approximate distance consistency supports long-horizon composition through waypoints, and that calibrated safety scores limit the expected number of true violations. Experiments across different navigation tasks show that CoGeL substantially reduces unsafe events while preserving strong long-horizon goal-reaching.

papers.title: Prioritized Multi-Constraint Coordination for Safe Multi-Robot Formation Navigation
papers.matched_title: Prioritized Multi-Constraint Coordination for Safe Multi-Robot Formation Navigation
papers.abstract:
Safe formation navigation requires a robot team to reach task goals while avoiding collisions and maintaining a desired formation geometry.
In this multi-robot cooperative task, task progress, collision avoidance, and formation maintenance often impose competing requirements on the team. 
Rather than treating these requirements as equally weighted objectives, we view them as prioritized constraints, where safety-critical constraints should take precedence over recoverable coordination errors such as temporary formation deformation. 
We formulate this setting as prioritized multi-constraint coordination and introduce a CTDE-based priority-conditioned actor--critic method.
During execution, each agent uses a decentralized actor conditioned on local observations and two online budgets that describe the current safety and formation regimes. 
During training, a multi-head centralized critic shares a common representation and predicts navigation return, safety violation, and formation degradation through three value heads. 
These estimates are used to update the online budgets and compute a hierarchical advantage for policy optimization. 
This design enables the team to avoid collisions, temporarily deform the formation when safety requires it, recover the desired structure after local conflicts, and continue goal-directed navigation.
We evaluate the method in VMAS-based formation-navigation scenarios with static and dynamic obstacles, and further demonstrate the learned policy  on a fleet of omnidirectional AGVs.
keywords: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems

papers.title: Adaptive Risk-Certified Event-Triggered Replanning for Dynamic Navigation
papers.matched_title: Adaptive Risk-Certified Event-Triggered Replanning for Dynamic Navigation
papers.abstract: Safe navigation in dynamic environments requires robots to plan under obstacle predictions whose errors are uncertain, non-stationary, and can induce rare but safety-critical failures. Existing control-barrier-function safety filters can reject immediately unsafe controls, but they provide little guidance on when the current finite-horizon planning mode itself is becoming unsafe as prediction uncertainty evolves. We propose Conformal Event-Triggered Risk-Certified Replanning (\emph{CERT-Replan}), a framework that uses calibrated barrier risk as an early-warning signal for replanning. CERT-Replan calibrates horizon-indexed obstacle-prediction residuals online and uses the resulting uncertainty radii to evaluate dynamic-obstacle safety margins. A one-step safety filter protects the next applied control, while a horizon-level risk monitor evaluates the upper-tail CVaR of predicted barrier-violation losses along the current MPC rollout. When this risk exceeds an allocated budget, CERT-Replan rejects the current planning mode and selects a lower-risk alternative, such as a different speed profile, corridor, or homotopy class, rather than repeatedly correcting the same nominal plan. In a non-stationary benchmark, CERT-Replan achieves an 83.3% collision reduction relative to the safety-filter-only baseline, while reducing average safety-filter intervention by 32.4%. Hardware-in-the-loop experiments further demonstrate onboard feasibility.

papers.title: Navigating the Clutter: Waypoint-Based Bi-Level Planning for Multi-Robot Systems
papers.matched_title: Navigating the Clutter: Waypoint-Based Bi-Level Planning for Multi-Robot Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-robot control in cluttered environments is a challenging problem that involves complex physical constraints, including robot–robot collisions, robot–obstacle collisions, and unreachable motions. Successful planning in such settings requires joint optimization over high-level task planning and low-level motion planning, as violations of physical constraints may arise from failures at either level. However, jointly optimizing task and motion planning is difficult due to the complex parameterization of low-level motion trajectories and the ambiguity of credit assignment across the two planning levels. In this paper, we propose a hybrid multi-robot control framework that jointly optimizes task and motion planning. To enable effective parameterization of low-level planning, we introduce waypoints, a simple yet expressive representation for motion trajectories. To address the credit assignment challenge, we adopt a curriculum-based training strategy with a modified RLVR algorithm that propagates motion feasibility feedback from the motion planner to the task planner. Experiments on BoxNet3D-Obs, a challenging multi-robot benchmark with dense obstacles and up to nine robots, show that our approach consistently improves task success over motion-agnostic and VLA-based baselines.

papers.title: PanoVine: Whole-Body Visuomotor Control for Soft Growing Vine Robot

papers.abstract: Vine robots, a class of soft, growing robots, are suitable for navigating complex and confined environments due to their compliant bodies and self-supporting growth mechanism. However, hysteresis, tether interactions, and deformations make them difficult to predict and model, which in turn limits the effectiveness of conventional planning and control approaches. In this work, we present a data-driven, vision-based control framework for the first autonomous vine robot system. Our system integrates 19 cameras distributed along the robot's body to provide comprehensive feedback of both the robot state and the surrounding environment. Using this rich whole-body vision feedback, we train an end-to-end visuomotor policy from demonstrations for closed-loop autonomous control in complex environments. The policy efficiently aggregates information from distributed sensing while maintaining robustness to inaccurate robot states and actuation. Experimental results demonstrate that the learned policy enables robust navigation and manipulation in challenging scenarios, including steering through branched structures, climbing up slopes, traversing unsupported terrain, reaching objects precisely, and maneuvering through confined spaces and obstacles.

papers.title: X-NavDP: Generalizing Navigation Diffusion Policy to Novel Behavior and Embodiments with Group Q-score Reweighted Matching
papers.matched_title: X-NavDP: Generalizing Navigation Diffusion Policy to Novel Behavior and Embodiments with Group Q-score Reweighted Matching
papers.abstract: Pretraining navigation diffusion policies rely on large-scale expert demonstrations. These data are typically generated by a fully-informed oracle planner suited to a single nominal robot. This limits the policy's generalization to diverse embodiments and challenging scenarios (e.g., escaping dead ends or detouring long obstacles) that demand diverse local reactive behaviors with only onboard local observations. Post-training the policy with reinforcement learning (RL) offers a principled remedy.However, previous RL for diffusion approaches lead to only marginal improvements. This is because the intractable likelihood of diffusion policies renders policy gradients unstable in addition to inefficient policy exploration. To address these challenges, we propose a data-efficient diffusion RL post-training framework - GQRM (Group Q-score Reweighted Matching). Our framework introduces two complementary designs: (i) a self-bootstrapped exploration strategy with behavior perturbation that preserves the pretrained policy prior, and (ii) a group Q-score normalization mechanism that computes per-trajectory values on each state for efficient reweighted score matching. By conducting distributed online RL training across heterogeneous embodiments, the resulting fine-tuned policy, X-NavDP, achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment visual navigation performance, improving the overall success rate from 61.20% to 84.28% in simulation and 10% to 65% in real-world hard cases.

papers.title: PathLift: Depth-Conditioned Metric Lifting for Visual-Navigation Priors
papers.matched_title: PathLift: Depth-Conditioned Metric Lifting for Visual-Navigation Priors
papers.abstract:
Generalist visual-navigation policies tell a robot which direction to go but not how far. A separate lifting step is needed at deployment to convert their unitless trajectory into a metric path that a controller can track; existing scalar lifters apply uniform scaling that misses per-waypoint corrections, while in-policy approaches that inject monocular depth into the policy inherit the prediction errors of the depth model near obstacles and at close range. 

We present PathLift, a per-waypoint depth-conditioned adapter that lifts a pre-trained visual-navigation policy by consuming an explicit, sensor-grade depth source (RGB-D, stereo, or projected LiDAR) and fitting per-waypoint magnitude and lateral residuals to a canonicalized prior. 

PathLift consistently improves closed-loop navigation across diverse visual-navigation policies in simulation and on a real wheeled robot under both stereo and LiDAR depth. By turning the policy's unitless intent into a depth-feasible metric path in a single feed-forward pass, the adapter lifts real-world success without test-time optimization.

papers.title: LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video
papers.matched_title: LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video
papers.abstract: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user's intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, language-conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate language-conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. This task is inherently non-trivial: viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intentions, and a valid motion may operate at different semantic granularity, from entering a room to looking around a corner, inspecting a visible object, or revealing an occluded detail. To model this structure, we mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.

papers.title: PROSE: Training-Free Egocentric Scene Registration with Vision-Language Models
papers.matched_title: PROSE: Training-Free Egocentric Scene Registration with Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Registering two captures of the same indoor space taken at different times underpins persistent spatial memory for robots and AR systems, yet the realistic version of this task is egocentric and its most scalable form is RGB-only. Head-mounted cameras yield blurry, fast-moving, partially overlapping views from which dense geometry is hard to recover. Classical registration leans on exactly the clean point clouds this setting lacks, while learned scene-graph methods require a pre-built or annotated graph and a trained matcher that we find brittle under egocentric data. We take a different route, using a pretrained vision-language model as the source of both scene understanding and cross-scan matching. Our method, PROSE (Prompted Scene rEgistration), lifts each RGB sequence into an object-level 3D scene graph using off-the-shelf foundation models for geometry, segmentation, and language, then prompts the same VLM to match object instances across the two RGB sequences. To make this matching tractable and reliable, we leverage object heights as a prior and verify each proposed match with a paired same/different query, then solve for the rigid transform by hypothesizing a candidate per matched object and selecting the one with the strongest geometric consensus. PROSE adds no learned parameters and requires no depth sensor, training, or annotated graph. On the egocentric Aria Digital Twin and Aria Everyday Activities benchmarks, it outperforms both geometric and learned scene-graph baselines in registration accuracy, on ground-truth and RGB-reconstructed point clouds alike, and the scene graph it produces transfers directly to downstream tasks.

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Absolute Pose Regression via Geometric Pose Proxy
papers.matched_title: Geometry-Aware Absolute Pose Regression via Geometric Pose Proxy
papers.abstract: Absolute pose regression (APR) provides an attractive route to real-time camera relocalization through a single feed-forward pass. However, the image-to-pose formulation hides the perspective and scene geometries that make localization well constrained, limiting its accuracy. To address this mismatch, we reformulate APR as a geometry-aware regression pipeline. The query image is first lifted into a scene pointmap, providing the downstream regressor with a geometric representation rather than appearance-only features. We then introduce a Gram-based pose proxy inspired by classical absolute pose estimation, where the network predicts a structured Gram matrix that jointly encodes perspective constraints and scene geometry. During training, we further propose geometry-guided pointmap augmentation, which constructs additional samples at novel viewpoints directly in the pointmap space. Compared with novel-view-synthesis-enhanced APR, it provides more geometry-focused samples without costly rendering or training an additional neural scene representation. Indoor and outdoor experiments show that our method substantially improves accuracy while retaining efficient feed-forward inference, achieving a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.title: FreeLoc: Online Floorplan Localization via Diffusion-Aided Pose Refinement
papers.matched_title: FreeLoc: Online Floorplan Localization via Diffusion-Aided Pose Refinement
papers.abstract: Floorplans provide compact and widely available geometric maps for indoor localization, but existing high-performing floorplan-based methods still convert them into dense scene-specific offline databases, tying accuracy, storage, and runtime to the sampling resolution of the discretized pose space. We present FreeLoc, an online RGB-based floorplan localization framework that treats the floorplan as a directly queryable geometric map. FreeLoc introduces an efficient online geometric querying and diffusion-aided refinement scheme, which retrieves plausible pose anchors through on-the-fly floorplan ray querying and refines them into accurate continuous pose estimates. For sequential localization, FreeLoc develops an online likelihood construction strategy that bridges single-frame localization and probabilistic temporal fusion by constructing likelihoods from coarse-sampled candidates and refined pose hypotheses, enabling histogram-filter-based temporal fusion without offline databases. Experiments demonstrate real-time online inference and state-of-the-art performance in both single-frame and sequential localization, while real-world results validate practical deployability in indoor robotic localization scenarios.

papers.title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
papers.matched_title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
papers.abstract:
Feature matching is a fundamental component of robotic perception systems, enabling visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matching methods formulate correspondence estimation as discrete confidence prediction over feature grids, inherently producing grid-aligned correspondences that require increasingly high-resolution feature maps for accurate localization, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead that limits real-time deployment on embedded robotic platforms.
We propose CoReMatch, a recurrent coordinate refinement framework for efficient semi-dense feature matching. CoReMatch reformulates semi-dense matching as iterative coordinate-space optimization and progressively refines correspondences through recurrent hidden-state propagation. At the coarse level, a Deep Aggregated Transformer performs efficient global correspondence refinement through recurrent coordinate updates. At the fine level, a lightweight local refinement module predicts sub-pixel coordinate corrections within compact feature windows for accurate geometric refinement. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate that CoReMatch achieves superior accuracy--efficiency trade-offs compared with state-of-the-art semi-dense matchers. In particular, CoReMatch achieves higher accuracy on MegaDepth while delivering over 10x faster inference than Efficient LoFTR on embedded edge devices. These results suggest that recurrent coordinate refinement provides an efficient and scalable formulation for real-time robotic perception.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
papers.matched_title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
papers.abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe "interaction bottleneck." Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a lightweight set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, and ETH3D, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

papers.title: G2G: Exploiting Intra-Group Geometry for Inter-Group Pose Estimation
papers.matched_title: G2G: Exploiting Intra-Group Geometry for Inter-Group Pose Estimation
papers.abstract:
Recovering the relative 6-DoF pose between two image groups underlies cross-sequence relocalization and multi-camera rig odometry.
Each group carries known intra-group geometry from visual odometry or rig calibration, and pretrained multi-view backbones already fuse such geometry into visual features.
Yet current models treat all views as an unstructured set, leaving cross-group reasoning as the missing piece.
We introduce \ours{}, which keeps the foundation model entirely frozen and adds three lightweight trainable modules to bridge the two groups: a perceiver resampler, a cross-group bridge with merged self-attention, and a multi-frame pose head.
The trainable footprint totals about 32M parameters, under 6\% of the full model, and is supervised only by relative poses.
Across four datasets that span indoor and outdoor simulation, real-world cross-season capture, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, \ours{} attains state-of-the-art accuracy on both tasks, while every baseline is retrained with its full original supervision.
Code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/G2G/}.

papers.title: LSPR: Init-Anchored Score-Based Multi-Camera Calibration for Indoor Robot Manipulation
papers.matched_title: LSPR: Init-Anchored Score-Based Multi-Camera Calibration for Indoor Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Multi-camera perception is a load-bearing pillar of indoor robot manipulation, yet current feed-forward 3D foundation models still provide only centimeter-level camera poses on cluttered manipulation rigs. In our RH20T setting, off-the-shelf COLMAP and RGB-D ICP can degrade rather than reliably improve WorldMirror-v2 initializations. We present latent score-based pose refinement (LSPR), a foundation-init-conditioned calibration method that repurposes diffusion from global pose generation into local residual refinement on the $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ tangent space. LSPR learns the score field of the residual pose-error distribution induced by a strong initializer: ground-truth rigs are corrupted by tangent-space perturbations covering the initializer's small-noise regime, and inference follows this field from the foundation initialization rather than sampling poses from noise. To make this local refinement reliable, LSPR combines score-level ensembling, hard-tier sample mining, and a confidence gate that falls back to the initializer under distribution shift. On held-out RH20T manipulation scenes, LSPR improves WorldMirror-v2 initializations from centimeter-level to sub-centimeter, sub-degree $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$-aligned accuracy, and these calibration gains transfer to downstream multi-view depth fusion.
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: CoLA: Robust Collaborative Perception with Linear Global Spatial Alignment
papers.matched_title: CoLA: Robust Collaborative Perception with Linear Global Spatial Alignment
papers.abstract: Collaborative perception enhances perceptual accuracy and range through multi-agent information sharing. To address spatial misalignment caused by pose error and communication latency in collaborative perception, existing methods enhance robustness by extending adaptive local feature fusion regions. However, computational bottleneck of basic operators prevents local windows from being extended to the global scope, making it difficult to cover complex and diverse perception scenarios. Accordingly, this paper proposes CoLA, a robust collaborative perception scheme which achieves global spatial semantic matching and alignment across agents with linear computational complexity. CoLA integrates Global Structure Rectification Module for global structure modeling and inter-agent denoising, and Ego-Anchored Gate Fusion module for semantic alignment and fusion. Furthermore, we design a patch-level structural consistency loss to suppress severe position jitter. Extensive experiments on both real-world and simulated datasets demonstrate that CoLA outperforms state-of-the-art methods under various noisy conditions.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: OptiGeo: Efficient Monocular Geometry for Embodied Perception in Optically Challenging Scenes
papers.matched_title: OptiGeo: Efficient Monocular Geometry for Embodied Perception in Optically Challenging Scenes
papers.abstract:
Monocular depth estimation has achieved strong open-domain generalization, yet reliable robotic deployment remains difficult in transparent, reflective, and specular environments, where depth sensors often produce missing or biased depth. Existing methods often handle such optical failures with scene-specific preprocessing, auxiliary modules, or post-hoc fine-tuning. While effective in constrained settings, these designs increase architectural redundancy and can over-specialize general geometry models to narrow optical scenarios. 
We revisit this problem as a localized failure mode within base-model training and identify sensor-induced supervision bias as a key bottleneck: models inherit sensor failure patterns from biased real-depth supervision in optically challenging regions.
We then introduce \textbf{OptiGeo}, a bias-aware training framework that rehabilitates biased real supervision using a clean-geometry teacher and residual-trimmed alignment. We redefine transparency-targeted rendering as a compact source of clean optical geometry, rather than a large domain-specific fine-tuning set. With only a small targeted rendering set, OptiGeo learns the geometric structure of transparent objects and regions, correcting local geometry distortions that real sensors cannot reliably supervise.
Despite only 30M parameters, OptiGeo outperforms substantially larger 300M-scale monocular models and billion-scale multi-view baselines on transparent-scene benchmarks, while remaining competitive on general zero-shot depth and boundary sharpness. Real-world navigation cases further validate its practicality as an efficient perception module in optically challenging scenes.

papers.title: Z3P: Zero-Shot 3D-Object Perception for Robotics
papers.matched_title: 3PTv2: Zero-Shot 3D-Object Perception Transformer for Robotics
papers.abstract: Tremendous progress has been made toward zero-shot, 3D-object-prompted perception tasks, including detection, segmentation, and 6D pose estimation. However, prior methods still struggle to see widespread use in robotics due to complexities such as challenging materials, dense clutter, and runtime. To address these limitations, we introduce Z3P, the first competitive end-to-end transformer architecture that performs zero-shot detection, segmentation, and pose estimation from single/multi-view RGB or RGB-D data and a 3D-object prompt. While previous methods use bounding boxes as an intermediate step between multiple models, Z3P operates as a single network that maintains an internal representation through persistent object tokens, allowing for better runtime and improved performance in densely cluttered environments with challenging materials. Across five robotic benchmarks (IPD, XYZ-IBD, ITODD-MV, T-ROBI, and ROBI), Z3P establishes a new state-of-the-art by becoming the first zero-shot method to outperform all prior zero-shot and object-specific approaches on detection and pose estimation. Finally, we demonstrate Z3P's utility as a foundation model for 3D-object perception, generalizing to multiple demanding robotic applications, including transparent object bin picking, sorting, car charging, and electronics assembly.
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: Cyclops: LiDAR as a Camera That Dreams in Color
papers.matched_title: Cyclops: LiDAR as a Camera That Dreams in Color
papers.abstract: Conventionally, robotic perception relies heavily on cameras due to the rich semantic texture they provide. However, their performance degrades significantly in low-light or high-dynamic-range environments. Conversely, while Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) captures illumination-invariant geometric and intensity properties, the resulting data are typically single-channel and sparse, creating a significant modality gap when applying vision models pre-trained on RGB datasets. In this paper, we propose Cyclops, a framework that translates sparse Non-Repetitive Scanning LiDAR (NRS-LiDAR) intensity into RGB video, enabling camera-free inference for all-day perception tasks. Our approach first converts sparse LiDAR intensity projections into dense representations via a frozen pre-trained densification module, serving as a geometrically rich source condition. The dense intensity latent is then transported toward the target RGB distribution through Latent Bridge Matching (LBM) with a learned velocity field in a few ODE integration steps. To mitigate inter-frame flickering, we inject prior-frame context via temporal attention layers and further formulate the velocity field as a policy optimized by a differentiable terminal reward that encourages terminal fidelity through backpropagation along the ODE trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized RGB, including those generated under near-dark conditions, enable standard RGB-based perception models to substantially outperform both LiDAR baselines and conventional cameras on semantic segmentation, lane detection, and point cloud colorization across diverse lighting conditions.

papers.title: MaD-PF: Modular and Differentiable Particle Filter for Cross-Environment SE(3) LiDAR Localization
papers.matched_title: MaD-PF: Modular and Differentiable Particle Filter for Cross-Environment SE(3) LiDAR Localization
papers.abstract:
Multi-modal robust localization requires estimating uncertainty over multiple pose hypotheses while adapting perception and motion models across environments and robotic platforms. Classical particle filters provide a principled Bayesian framework for this problem, but their manually specified models and discrete resampling operations limit integration into end-to-end trainable robotic systems, while learning-based localization approaches typically lack the modularity and generalizability. Differentiable particle filters promise to combine these two worlds by replacing filtering components with differentiable alternatives, but existing methods remain confined to either planar state spaces, visual or simulated observations, or single-platform evaluation. We present the first end-to-end differentiable particle filter capable of real-world cross-environment SE(3) LiDAR localization by using a unit dual quaternion formulation, 3D-LiDAR observations, and differentiable motion, observation, and resampling modules. Within this framework, we thoroughly compare different submodules and propose improvements that demonstrate increased robustness on held-out datasets and, in parallel, \qty{89}{\percent} latency reduction for the observation model. We evaluate the framework on real-world LiDAR data, demonstrating zero-shot RMSE of \qty{0.398}{m} or better in unknown environments, on different robotic platforms, or both, and we outperform SotA learning-based localization systems requiring $2.5 \times$ less training time.
Project Website: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/MaD-PF/
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: AmodalBox: Automated 3D Bounding Box Annotation under Partial Visibility
papers.matched_title: AmodalBox: Automated 3D Bounding Box Annotation under Partial Visibility
papers.abstract: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observation remains a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose AmodalBox, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, AmodalBox robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, AmodalBox propagates anchor-based alignments for dynamic instances and aggregates multi-frame evidence for static objects. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from AmodalBox improves performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 mAP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD).
keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: Functional-SLAM: Interaction-Aware Mapping with Online Functional Scene Graphs
papers.matched_title: Functional-SLAM: Interaction-Aware Mapping with Online Functional Scene Graphs
papers.abstract:
Existing SLAM systems lack modeling of the functional relations required for fine-grained robotic interaction. Functional 3D scene graphs can represent relations between objects and interaction elements, but existing methods rely on offline reconstruction, making them inadequate for real-time interaction in real-world exploration. 
To address this limitation, we propose Functional-SLAM, the first framework that continuously and recursively maintains a functional scene graph as an online SLAM state.
The framework combines anchor-keyframe geometry with functional-context constraints for persistent node maintenance, accumulates multi-frame evidence through temporal relations to commit stable functional edges, and supplements visual loop-closure candidates with functional topology in scenes with repetitive appearance or degraded texture.
Experiments show that Functional-SLAM efficiently constructs stable functional maps online, substantially improving runtime over offline methods while maintaining highly competitive accuracy. Compared with peer SLAM systems, it further improves pose estimation accuracy through functional-topology-assisted loop closure.

papers.title: RoMo-GS: Efficient Online 3D Gaussian Splatting for Robot Mapping via Exposure-Integrated Motion Blur
papers.matched_title: RoMo-GS: Efficient Online 3D Gaussian Splatting for Robot Mapping via Exposure-Integrated Motion Blur
papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is emerging as a practical way to build a representation for robotics applications. However, deploying it on real-world platforms exposes multiple challenges. Rapid maneuvers of a robot induce motion-blurred images, which corrupt the reconstructed geometry and cause camera pose drift. Furthermore, the number of Gaussians grows without bound during continuous online mapping. In this study, we present RoMo-GS, an online 3DGS system designed to address these challenges. Instead of averaging N discrete sub-frames as in prior motion blur-aware 3DGS, we analytically integrate each projected Gaussian over the exposure interval, yielding an O(1) complexity per Gaussian. Building on this, we bound the Gaussians' growth with a Hessian-based pruning score, while jointly refining pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam and an online LM step over the Gaussians. On multiple public datasets and a self-collected dataset, RoMo-GS matches or exceeds offline deblurring 3DGS methods in rendering quality while training 15--150x faster, and operates online at competitive quality with about 20% fewer Gaussians than the online 3DGS baseline.
keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control

papers.title: Learning Contact Representation for Leg Odometry
papers.matched_title: Learning Contact Representation for Leg Odometry
papers.abstract: Leg odometry relies on the assumption that the velocity of a foot in stance is zero with respect to the world, which makes accurate contact detection a critical subproblem. Many approaches classify contact using ground reaction force (GRF) sensors at the foot tip, yet these sensors are not available on all legged robots and remain unresponsive to disturbances such as slippage while the foot is still in contact. Approaches without GRF sensing instead rely on heuristic pseudo-labels, model-based foot-velocity assumptions, or supervised contact learning. In this study, we propose a self-supervised representation learning framework for contact detection that uses only standard proprioceptive sensing (joint encoders and IMU) and requires neither force sensors nor contact labels. A denoising autoencoder is trained on kinematic features, a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model is fitted in the learned latent space, and its posterior is used as a continuous stance belief that scales the zero-velocity measurement covariance of an error-state Kalman filter. Experiments in simulation and on real-world terrain show that our framework yields the lowest odometry error among supervised and probabilistic baselines, and that higher pseudo-label classification accuracy does not translate into better downstream odometry. Our code and dataset are publicly available.

papers.title: GINIO: A Geometric SO(3)-Equivariant Interface for Neural Inertial Odometry
papers.matched_title: GINIO: A Geometric SO(3)-Equivariant Interface for Neural Inertial Odometry
papers.abstract: Neural inertial odometry increasingly uses networks as learned measurements inside filtering pipelines. Such measurements should transform consistently under arbitrary IMU mounting conventions: their mean must transform as a vector, and their covariance must transform congruently as a second-order tensor. We present \textbf{GINIO}, a geometric \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\)-equivariant interface for neural inertial odometry under arbitrary rotations of the IMU measurement frame. Given calibrated IMU windows, our framework predicts a motion measurement and uncertainty obeying these tensorial laws. To support efficient sensor-frame learning, we introduce Last-Frame Alignment (LFA), a deterministic preprocessing step that is provably equivalent to world-frame training for \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\)-equivariant predictors. The connected estimator tracks sensor-local states such as IMU bias, separating nuisance estimation from the geometric law enforced by the learned measurement. We instantiate the same interface in filter-connected NIO, AirIO-style recurrent aerial prediction, EqNIO-style full-\(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) canonicalization, and ResNet-style temporal backbones. On TLIO, GINIO achieves 2.018 m ID/\(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) ATE while EqNIO degrades to 76.389 m, using \(11.6\times\) fewer FLOPs. On NanoBench, our AirIO-style instantiation improves ATE from 5.579 m to 1.430 m without external attitude input, and our ResNet-style instantiation reaches 0.581 m ATE versus 0.645 m for ResNet1D. On Fetch, GINIO reduces unseen physical-remount ATE from 8.15 m to 0.50 m without retraining.

papers.title: PLATO: Privileged Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations for Neural Inertial Preintegration
papers.matched_title: PLATO: Preintegration-Based Likelihood Maximization from Accurate Trajectory Observations for Neural Inertial Odometry
papers.abstract:
Neural inertial odometry has demonstrated strong potential for motion estimation in challenging environments, yet inertial-only preintegration remains sensitive to IMU bias and uncertainty.
To this end, this paper introduces \textbf{PLATO}:~\emph{Privileged Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations}, a likelihood-based framework that leverages accurate trajectory observations to jointly learn IMU bias dynamics modeled by a neural ordinary differential equation~(NODE) and gyroscope and accelerometer noise covariances.
Optimization exploits the sparse structure of the negative log-likelihood, with IMU noise-parameter gradients computed by forward differentiation.
A tailored double-adjoint scheme couples a discrete invariant-error adjoint with a continuous-time adjoint for the bias NODE, enabling memory-efficient likelihood optimization over the nested bias-dynamics and IMU-preintegration rollouts.
Validation on EuRoC shows improved performance, and underwater robot experiments demonstrate applicability under intermittent lighting failures and visual degradation.
keywords: Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics
Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision

papers.title: Language as a Sensor: Calibrated Spatial Belief Estimation in 3D Scenes from Natural Language
papers.matched_title: Language as a Sensor: Calibrated Spatial Belief Estimation in 3D Scenes from Natural Language
papers.abstract: Robots deployed in human-centric environments routinely receive natural-language descriptions of spatial information (“I left my backpack on the table”) that reference parts of the world beyond their perceptual field of view. Traditional metric-semantic mapping ignores this signal, while off-the-shelf multimodal models remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning and are not directly amenable to fusion with other sensor modalities. To convert language observations into a calibrated spatial distribution, we train a Language Sensor Model (LSM) that maps each utterance and its scene-graph context to a multimodal distribution, with mixture weights encoding referential ambiguity (e.g., “which table”) and component covariances encoding spatial uncertainty (e.g., where “on the table” the target lies). We then introduce VL-Map (Vision-Language Metric-Semantic Mapping), a probabilistic framework that treats these language predictions as stochastic observations and fuses them with onboard perception within a unified belief map. On the VLA-3D benchmark as well as on a real-world mobile robot, LSM is the only language predictor whose covariance estimates remain within the calibrated regime; fused into VL-Map, it leads to more accurate predictions of the target object location (~70% more probability mass on the true target compared to the strongest foundation-model baseline).
